cards.text: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, is writing to the believers in Philippi, and he's writing it in chains (Phil 1:1, 7). Now he wants them to know how his circumstances have turned out. So lean in, friend, because here comes the update.

cards.question: Paul's in chains. So what does he say his circumstances have actually done for the gospel?
Paul says that because of all this, one group now clearly knows he's in chains for Christ, along with everyone else. Which group does he name?

cards.text: So the guards know it, and everybody else knows it: Paul is in chains for Christ. Now watch what those chains do to the other believers.

cards.question: Seeing Paul in chains, most of the brothers get scared and go quiet about the word. True or false?

cards.text: Most of the brothers are confident in the Lord by Paul's chains, and they dare more greatly to speak the word without fear. It's like one coworker speaks up in the toughest meeting of the year, and suddenly the WHOLE room finds its voice.
But Paul's honest about something. Not everybody preaching Christ is doing it for the same reason.

cards.question: Paul says some people preach Christ out of goodwill. What does he say drives the others?
The ones preaching Christ out of goodwill do it in ___, knowing Paul is appointed for the defense of the gospel.

cards.text: The other crowd preaches Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely. And they think it'll get to Paul somehow.

cards.question: What do the insincere preachers suppose they can do to Paul?

answers.text: Add to the distress of his chains

cards.question: Paul asks, "What then is the issue?" What does he say is the thing that matters?

answers.text: That his own name is cleared

cards.question: Whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached, and in this Paul ___.

cards.text: And Paul says he will continue to rejoice. Some folks are preaching out of rivalry, and he just KEEPS rejoicing. Friend, I can't stay that happy when my oven timer goes off early.
Paul's still in chains, but he's not guessing about how this ends. He says he knows how all this distress is going to turn out.

cards.question: Paul says he knows his distress will turn out for his ___.
Paul says his deliverance will come through two things. What are they?

answers.text: Their prayers and the Spirit's provision
Their gifts and the guards' kindness
His defense and the court's mercy

cards.text: Paul eagerly expects and hopes he won't be ashamed in any way. He wants complete boldness, so that Christ will be exalted in his body.

cards.question: Paul hopes Christ will be exalted in his body only if he gets to keep living. True or false?

cards.text: Then Paul says it plain: "For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain." Read that one twice, friend. I'll wait.
But if he goes on living in the body, Paul says, that means fruitful labor. So now he's asking himself which one to choose.

cards.question: Paul asks himself which he'll choose, living or dying. What's his answer?

answers.text: He'll wait for the court to rule

cards.text: Paul says he's torn between the two. I get torn between chocolate chips and sprinkles, and I think Paul sounds calmer about life and death than I do at the topping bar.

cards.question: Paul says he desires to depart. What does he say departing would mean for him?
Paul calls departing to be with Christ far better. But he says remaining in the body is more necessary for someone. Who?
Paul is convinced he will remain and continue with the Philippians for their progress and joy in the faith. True or false?

cards.text: And when he comes to them again, Paul says their exultation in Christ Jesus will resound on account of him. He's basically telling them, don't give my seat away yet.
Then Paul turns from his own news to the Philippians. He's got one big ask for them.

cards.question: What is Paul's big ask for the Philippians?

answers.text: Live in a way worthy of the gospel
Come and visit him in his chains
Send a message to the palace guard

cards.question: Whether Paul comes and sees them or only hears about them, he wants to know they stand firm in one ___, contending together as one for the faith of the gospel.

cards.text: He wants them standing firm without being frightened in any way by those who oppose them. Picture the other team running their mouths all game, and your side just shrugs and keeps playing.

cards.question: Right after telling the Philippians not to be frightened by those who oppose them, Paul says, "This is a clear sign," and it's from God. A sign of what?

answers.text: Their opponents' destruction and their salvation
Their opponents' victory and their defeat
Their own pride and their weakness

cards.text: Then Paul tells them what's been granted to them on behalf of Christ.

cards.question: It has been granted to the Philippians on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to ___ for Him.
Paul says the struggle the Philippians are encountering is a different one from his own. True or false?

cards.text: They saw Paul's struggle, and now they hear he's still in it. It's the same struggle they're in, and friend, I know from my drawer days how much it helps to be in the hard stuff together.

findings.problem: Card 4 is mostly a recap. Card 3 already answered that the palace guard and everyone else know Paul is in chains for Christ (1:13), and card 4 tells it again before moving on. Only its last sentence moves the passage forward.

The joke doesn't click. In 1:15-18, people deliberately preach out of rivalry and want to add to Paul's distress, and he keeps rejoicing. An oven timer going off early isn't someone working against you, and it isn't clear why it would be upsetting. A stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 5 of its 8 choice cards are multiple choice, against 2 fill in the blank and 1 true or false.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: "So now he's asking himself which one to choose" decides who 'So what shall I choose?' (1:22) is addressed to. In a letter to the Philippians, the text leaves the audience of this question open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question opens with "Paul asks himself which he'll choose," which again decides who the question in 1:22 is addressed to. The text leaves that open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Rest from his labor" can be argued as right. Verse 1:22 says that living on in the body means fruitful labor, so a baker could reason that departing means rest from that labor.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The question says "This is a clear sign," and it's from God, which states that the sign is from God. In 1:28 ('a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God'), the text leaves open what 'it' refers to: the sign, the salvation, or the whole thing.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Across the walkthrough, Papa Dorin is mostly pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny. Many story cards have no personality beyond the retelling, for example stop 3 cards 1 and 6 and stop 2 cards 1 and 4. The few jokes are mild, and one of them (stop 1 card 14) doesn't land.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
